---
title: "Commands you can take back"
---

Ctrl+Z is the most forgiving key on your keyboard, and an app can only offer it
when every action it performs knows how to reverse itself. This chapter builds a
counter with multi-level undo: click Add a few times, click Undo the same number
of times, and the counter is back at zero. The class that remembers the history
comes first, and its tests come before it.

## Red before green {#sec-undo-experiment}

{{< exercise undo-counter tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `homework/`, in a folder
   called `undo-counter`.

2. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`. The page you copied in has no
   `add` line on it any more.

3. Create `src/undo-stack.test.ts` and write the first sentence about a class
   that does not exist:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { UndoStack } from './undo-stack';

   describe('UndoStack', () => {
     it('starts empty', () => {
       const stack = new UndoStack<string>();

       expect(stack.size).toBe(0);
     });

   ```

4. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    ❯ src/undo-stack.test.ts (0 test)

   ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Suites 1 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

    FAIL  src/undo-stack.test.ts [ src/undo-stack.test.ts ]
   Error: Cannot find module './undo-stack' imported from
   /home/you/creative-coding-2/homework/undo-counter/src/undo-stack.test.ts
    ❯ src/undo-stack.test.ts:2:1
   ```

Read the count at the bottom: `Tests  no tests`. Vitest never reached your `it`,
because the import at the top of the file had nowhere to go, and a file that
cannot even load counts as a **failed suite** rather than a failed test.

5. Now write the smallest class that answers that one test, in
   `src/undo-stack.ts`:

   ```ts
   export class UndoStack<T> {
     private itemList: T[] = [];

     get size(): number {
       return this.itemList.length;
     }
   }
   ```

   `npm test` turns green: `Tests  1 passed (1)`.

6. Add the second sentence below the first `it`, and save:

   ```ts
     it('gives back the item that was pushed last', () => {
       const stack = new UndoStack<string>();
       stack.push('a');

       expect(stack.pop()).toBe('a');
     });
   ```

   VS Code underlines `push` and `pop` in red before you run anything, and
   `npx tsc --noEmit` says why:

   ```text
   src/undo-stack.test.ts(13,11): error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'UndoStack<string>'.
   ```

   Vitest does not type-check, so it runs the file anyway and hits the same

   ```text
    FAIL  src/undo-stack.test.ts > UndoStack > gives back the item that was pushed last
   ```

## Write the sentence, then make it true {#sec-undo-test-first}

Writing a test that cannot pass yet has a name: **test-first** work. The test is
a sentence about what the class should do, you watch it fail, and then you write
just enough code to make the sentence true. The failing run is the step people
skip, and it is the one that proves the test is really watching.

A test written after the code has a habit of describing whatever the code
happens to do, bugs included. You already know the answer while you type the
expectation, so you type that answer in.

Keep the loop small: one `it`, watch it fail, make it pass, next `it`.
`npm run test:watch` in a second terminal shows the failure on every save.

## A stack that never heard of commands {#sec-undo-generic}

Your class pushes and pops, and it can report its size. Five more sentences
finish it, and you write them the same way, one at a time:

* `pop()` on an empty stack gives back `undefined`
* three pushed items come back newest first
* `clear()` leaves the size at 0
* `items` lists two pushed items with the newest last
* pushing onto the array that `items` handed out leaves `size` unchanged

The first two already pass on the code you have, which is fine: they pin that
behavior down for later. The last three ask for two new members, and here is the
class once all five are green:

```ts
export class UndoStack<T> {
  private itemList: T[] = [];

  push(item: T): void {
    this.itemList.push(item);
  }

  pop(): T | undefined {
    return this.itemList.pop();
  }

  clear(): void {
    this.itemList = [];
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.itemList.length;
  }

  get items(): T[] {
    return this.itemList.slice();
  }
}
```

That is the `Stack<T>` of the last chapter without `peek`, plus `clear` and
`items`. The private array is named `itemList` here so that the getter can take
the name `items`, the same trick the bracelet used. That getter hands out a
copy, so nobody can push into the history behind the class's back, and it comes
with the newest item last, which is the order the page lists them in.

With seven `it` blocks in one `describe`, move
`const stack = new UndoStack<string>();` into a `beforeEach` above them and
declare `let stack: UndoStack<string>;` next to it. Expected result:

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  7 passed (7)
```

This app stores nothing but commands in the stack, so why not write
`push(item: Command)` and be done with the angle brackets? Because a container
that names its content can only ever be used by one app. The moment `UndoStack`
mentions `Command`, a chat app cannot use it for messages and your own tests
cannot use it for strings. Nothing inside the class calls a method on its items,
so `T` needs no constraint either.

Your test file is the proof. Every test in `src/undo-stack.test.ts` uses
`new UndoStack<string>()`, and strings know nothing about counters. Keep it
that way. In the next part you will pull the array out of this class and put
hand-built nodes in its place, and every test you write today has to stay green
afterwards.

## An action that knows how to undo itself {#sec-undo-command}

The counter has one number in it. Adding 3 means `value + 3`, and taking that
back means `value - 3`, so the stack has to remember enough to run the second
line. A number alone does not say whether it was added or subtracted.

Wrap each action in an object instead. The **command pattern** gives every
action a class that carries what it needs and knows both directions. Write
`src/command.ts`:

```ts
export abstract class Command {
  abstract execute(current: number): number;
  abstract undo(current: number): number;
  abstract describe(): string;
}
```

Each method takes the current value and returns the new one. `describe()` gives
the short text the history list shows.

Test first again, in `src/command.test.ts`:

```ts
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { AddCommand } from './command';

describe('AddCommand', () => {
  it('adds its delta to the current value', () => {
    const command = new AddCommand(3);

    expect(command.execute(5)).toBe(8);
  });
});
```

Then the class that makes it true, in the same `src/command.ts`:

```ts
export class AddCommand extends Command {
  constructor(private readonly delta: number) {
    super();
  }

  execute(current: number): number {
    return current + this.delta;
  }

  undo(current: number): number {
    return current - this.delta;
  }

  describe(): string {
    return `+ ${this.delta}`;
  }
}
```

The delta is private and `readonly`. Once a command is built it is a record of
something that happened, and nobody gets to edit it.

Add two more tests for `AddCommand`, one for `undo(8)` giving `5` and one for
`describe()` giving `'+ 3'`. Then repeat the round for `SubtractCommand`. Its
`execute` subtracts and its `undo` adds, and `describe()` gives `'- 2'` for a
delta of 2. Six tests in that file, and this is what both files together
report:

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  13 passed (13)
```

Since the polymorphism chapter the rule has been one class per file. These three
share `src/command.ts` as an exception: they are one family of tiny classes that
is never useful apart, and the file carries the family name.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From last year's exam sheet

"Yes, you could do it with a signed delta. Don't. The point is the pattern:
every command carries its own undo."

For a counter, one class holding `-2` really would do the job. The pattern earns
its keep as soon as the actions stop being arithmetic: in a drawing app one
command adds a circle and another changes a color, with no single number to
flip. Each of them knows how to take itself back, and the undo stack never
changes.
:::

::: {.research title="Three things the wiring needs"}
The page you copied in shows the counter in an element you have not met yet, and
it hands your click listener whatever the user typed into the delta field. MDN
answers all three questions.

1. The value sits in `<output id="value">0</output>`. What is the `<output>`
   element meant for, and which type name goes into
   `document.querySelector<...>('#value')` for it?
2. The delta field is `<input type="number" min="1" step="1">`. Does the browser
   keep a value like `2.5` away from your click listener, or does
   `valueAsNumber` hand it to you anyway?
3. `Number.isNaN` catches the empty field and says nothing about `2.5`. Which
   `Number` function answers whether a value is a whole number, and what does it
   give back for the string `'2'`?

For the exam, the whole-number check has to be in your head: reading a number
out of a form and refusing the bad ones turns up in every second exercise.
:::

## Exercise: a counter that forgets nothing {#sec-undo-exercise}

Both modules are tested, and no class in them has ever seen the page.
Everything below happens in `src/index.ts`, the only file in this project that
touches the DOM.

1. Open the `index.html` you copied in and find the seven elements the next
   steps use: the `<output>` with the value, the delta input, the Add and
   Subtract buttons, the Undo button, the paragraph with `id="message"`, and the
   empty `<ol id="history">`.

2. Replace `src/index.ts`. It starts with the imports:

   ```ts
   import './styles.css';
   import { AddCommand, type Command, SubtractCommand } from './command';
   import { UndoStack } from './undo-stack';
   ```

   `Command` is used only as a type here, never with `new`, and Biome wants the
   `type` keyword right in front of such a name. `npm run check:fix` puts it
   there.

3. Look up all seven elements with `querySelector`, using the type name for
   `<output>` from the research task, and stop the app with one `if` and a
   `throw new Error(...)` when any of them is missing.

4. The whole state of this app is two lines:

   ```ts
   const undoStack = new UndoStack<Command>();
   let value = 0;
   ```

   `UndoStack<Command>` fills the hole in the class with your own type, so
   `pop()` hands back a `Command | undefined` and TypeScript knows that
   `describe()` and `undo()` exist on it.

5. Write a `render()` helper that draws everything the state says:

   * the value goes into the output element as text
   * the Undo button is disabled while `undoStack.size` is 0
   * the history list is emptied with `replaceChildren()` and refilled with one
     `<li>` per item of `undoStack.items`, each showing that command's
     `describe()`

   The oldest command is the top line of the list, and the bottom line is the
   one Undo takes back next.

6. Write a `readDelta()` helper that returns `number | undefined`. It reads
   `valueAsNumber` from the delta input, and when that is not a whole number of
   at least 1 it writes `'Please enter a whole number of at least 1.'` into the
   message paragraph and returns `undefined`. Otherwise it clears the message
   and returns the number. Use the check from the research task here.

7. Write a `run(command: Command)` helper with the three lines every new action
   needs: hand the current value to `execute` and keep what comes back, push the
   command onto the undo stack, call `render()`.

8. Give the Add button a `click` listener that calls `readDelta()`, returns
   right away when the answer is `undefined`, and otherwise calls
   `run(new AddCommand(delta))`. The Subtract button gets the same listener with
   `SubtractCommand`.

9. Give the Undo button a `click` listener that pops the stack, does nothing
   when the stack was empty, and otherwise hands the current value to that
   command's `undo` and keeps what comes back. Then `render()`.

10. Call `render()` once at the end of the file, so the fresh page shows 0 and a
    disabled Undo button.

11. Run `npm start` and check all of it. Expected results:

    * Add with a delta of 3, twice: the value shows 6 and the history has two
      lines reading `+ 3`
    * Subtract with a delta of 2: the value shows 4 and a third line reads `- 2`
    * Undo three times: 6, then 3, then 0, with the history shrinking line by
      line and the Undo button going gray at the end
    * a delta of `2.5` or an empty field: the message appears, the value stays,
      and no line joins the history

12. Run `npm test` and expect `Tests  13 passed (13)`. Add the `verify` script
    with its three checks to `package.json` as in every new app, run
    `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Redo.** Keep a second `UndoStack<Command>` next to the first one. The Undo
listener pushes the command it popped onto the redo stack, and a Redo button
pops from there, runs `execute` again, and pushes the command back onto the undo
stack. Any new Add or Subtract calls `clear()` on the redo stack, because the
history just took a different turn. Add a Redo button to `index.html` and
disable it while the redo stack is empty.

**ResetCommand.** A third subclass in `src/command.ts` that sets the value to 0.
It cannot know in advance what it is replacing, so `execute` stores the value it
was handed in a private field and `undo` gives that value back. Write the test
first: `execute(7)` is `0`, and `undo(0)` right after that is `7`. Its `undo`
never looks at the number it is handed, and TypeScript refuses a parameter that
is never read, so name that one `_current`: an underscore in front says you left
it out on purpose. Then add a Reset button to the page and send the new command
through the same `run` helper.
:::
